blocks.text: For centuries, carpets were the furniture of a Turkmen home. In the felt tent of [A1 unit 10](a1-u10-culture) they covered the floor, hung at the door and served as bags of every size for clothes and bedding, and special pieces dressed the camels on great occasions such as weddings. Encyclopaedia Iranica lists them: the large main carpet on the floor of the tent, storage bags large and small, door hangings and bands for the tent, and animal trappings made for great occasions.

Their best-known feature is the *göl*: a medallion, often an octagon divided into quarters, repeated in rows across the field of the carpet. Each of the great Turkmen tribes, among them the *Teke*, *Ýomut*, *Salyr*, *Saryk* and *Ärsary*, wove its own göls, so a göl has long been read as a tribe's emblem. Specialists add a caution: designs travelled between tribes and changed over time, so today a carpet is attributed by its knots, wool and colours as much as by its göls.

The colour that strikes most visitors is red. Iranica describes red as the dominant colour of Turkmen carpets, taken from the root of the madder plant; depending on how the wool was dyed and fixed, with mordants such as dried yogurt or alum, it runs from a dark brownish red to bright scarlet. Dark blue, white and touches of other colours set off the göls. The wool came from the family's own sheep. Synthetic dyes appeared around 1910 and are common today, but natural dyes have not disappeared.

Carpets were woven at home, mostly by women, and girls learned from their mothers. UNESCO, which added traditional Turkmen carpet making to its list of the intangible heritage of humanity in 2019, notes that the skills are still handed down within the family, and that special carpets are woven for the birth of a child, for weddings, and for prayer and mourning.

Turkmenistan has put the carpet among its national symbols. The red band at the side of the flag carries five göls, one for each of five major tribes, the *Teke*, *Ýomut*, *Saryk*, *Çowdur* and *Ärsary*, above two olive branches that were added in 1997. Since 1992 the last Sunday of May has been Carpet Day, a national holiday with exhibitions and awards for weavers, and Ashgabat has a carpet museum with about two thousand pieces.

blocks.title: Talking about a craft
blocks.text: The general present suits a craft, what people do as a rule: *Ejäm haly dokar*, my mother weaves carpets. *Haly* is the word you met in [A1 unit 10](a1-u10): *Öýde owadan haly bar*.
With this unit's general present, you can read this:

blocks.tk: Biziň öýümizde uly gyzyl haly bar. Ejäm we uýam haly dokarlar. Ejäm her gün dokar, ýöne täze haly entek taýýar däl. Her göl bir taýpanyň belgisi. Türkmenistanyň baýdagynda hem bäş göl bar.
blocks.en: In our home there is a big red carpet. My mother and my sister weave carpets. My mother weaves every day, but the new carpet isn't ready yet. Each göl is the mark of a tribe. There are five göls on the flag of Turkmenistan, too.

vocab.en: göl, the medallion of a Turkmen carpet

questions.q: What do the five göls on the flag stand for?
options: the five days of Carpet Day
questions.explain: One göl for each of five major tribes: the *Teke*, *Ýomut*, *Saryk*, *Çowdur* and *Ärsary*.

questions.q: Where does the red of Turkmen carpets traditionally come from?
options: the root of the madder plant
questions.explain: Madder root gives the reds; synthetic dyes came in only around 1910.

questions.q: In the reading, who weaves carpets?
questions.explain: *Ejäm we uýam haly dokarlar*: my mother and my sister weave carpets.
